message.content:
Below is a concise overview of the key rights and protections you have as a tenant in Texas. (This is general information and not legal advice; for specific situations you may want to consult an attorney or a local tenant‑rights organization.) | Category | What You’re Entitled To | How to Exercise It | |----------|------------------------|--------------------| | **Security Deposit** | • Landlord may charge up to **one month’s rent** for a furnished unit and **two months’ rent** for an unfurnished unit.
• Deposit must be returned within **30 days** after you move out, minus any lawful deductions. | • Keep a written move‑in inspection report.
• Request a written itemized statement of deductions if the landlord keeps any portion. | | **Habitability** | • Landlord must keep the premises in a safe, livable condition: functioning plumbing, heating, electrical, structural integrity, pest control, etc. | • Report problems in writing (email or letter).
• If the landlord fails to fix, you may withhold rent, repair and deduct, or terminate the lease (see below). | | **Rent Payment** | • Rent is due on the date specified in the lease. | • Pay on time; keep receipts or bank records. | | **Lease Termination** | • **Notice Requirements**:
 – **Month‑to‑month**: 30‑day written notice.
 – **Fixed‑term**: 30‑day notice if you’re breaking the lease early (unless the lease says otherwise).
 – **Landlord termination**: 30‑day notice for non‑payment or lease violation. | • Provide written notice (email or certified mail). | | **Right to Quiet Enjoyment** | • Landlord cannot enter without **reasonable notice** (usually 24 hours) unless it’s an emergency. | • Keep a log of any unannounced entries. | | **Discrimination** | • Texas law (and federal Fair Housing Act) prohibits discrimination based on race, color, religion, sex, national origin, disability, familial status, or source of income. | • File a complaint with the Texas Commission on Human Rights or the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD). | | **Repair and Deduct** | • If the landlord fails to repair a major issue, you may repair it yourself and deduct the cost from rent, provided you give notice and keep receipts. | • Document the problem, send notice, then repair. | | **Rent Increase** | • Landlords can raise rent at the end of a lease term or with proper notice (usually 30 days for month‑to‑month). | • Review lease terms; negotiate if possible. | | **Eviction Process** | • Landlord must follow the Texas eviction procedure: serve a **Notice to Pay Rent or Quit** (10 days) or **Notice to Cure or Quit** (10 days) for lease violations.
• If you fail to comply, the landlord files an unlawful detainer action. | • Respond promptly; keep records of all communications. | | **Security Deposit Deductions** | • Landlord may deduct for: unpaid rent, damage beyond normal wear, cleaning, lost keys, etc. | • Request an itemized list; dispute any unjustified deductions. | | **Utilities** | • Lease must specify who pays utilities. | • Verify utility bills and keep copies. | | **Subletting / Assignment** | • Many leases require landlord approval; Texas law does not prohibit subletting but requires the landlord to act reasonably. | • Get written permission; keep a copy. | | **Maintenance of Common Areas** | • Landlord must maintain common areas (hallways, elevators, parking lots) in a safe condition. | • Report issues; keep a log. | | **Right to Privacy** | • Landlord must respect your privacy; they can’t enter without notice except emergencies. | • Keep a record of any unauthorized entries. | | **Legal Remedies** | • If the landlord violates your rights, you can: file a complaint with the Texas Commission on Human Rights, sue for damages, or seek an injunction. | • Keep all documentation (photos, receipts, correspondence). | ### Quick Tips for Protecting Your Rights 1. **Read the Lease Carefully** – Understand all terms, especially those about rent, deposits, maintenance, and notice periods. 2. **Document Everything** – Photos, videos, written notices, and receipts help protect you if disputes arise. 3. **Communicate in Writing** – Email or certified mail provides a paper trail. 4. **Know the Law** – Texas Property Code Sections 92.001–92.019 cover security deposits; Sections 92.101–92.109 cover habitability; Section 92.111 covers notice requirements. 5. **Seek Help Early** – If you suspect discrimination or a serious habitability issue, contact the Texas Commission on Human Rights or a local tenant‑rights group. --- #### Useful Resources - **Texas Commission on Human Rights** – [https://www.tchra.texas.gov](https://www.tchra.texas.gov) - **Texas Attorney General – Consumer Protection** – [https://www.texasattorneygeneral.gov](https://www.texasattorneygeneral.gov) - **U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD)** – [https://www.hud.gov](https://www.hud.gov) - **Texas Tenants’ Rights Guide** – Many local nonprofits publish free guides; search online for “Texas tenant rights guide PDF.” If you have a specific situation (e.g., a landlord refusing to return a deposit, a repair that hasn’t been fixed, or a notice of eviction), let me know and I can give more tailored guidance.
